title: Stories About God's Kingdom
overview: Jesus tells a series of short stories about the "kingdom of heaven," meaning God's rule breaking into the world, and is then turned away by his own hometown.

parts.label: Seed on four soils (vv. 1-9, 18-23)
parts.note: A farmer scatters seed by hand, so some lands on a hard path, some on thin soil over rock, some among thorns and some on good ground. Jesus later explains that the seed is his message and the soils are kinds of listeners: some never take it in, some quit when it costs them, some let worry and money crowd it out, and some let it grow into a large harvest.

parts.label: Why speak in stories (vv. 10-17)
parts.note: Jesus says people who welcome what they hear will be given more understanding, while those who shut it out will lose even the little they had. He quotes the prophet Isaiah, who was told his own people would hear without understanding, and tells his followers they are seeing what earlier prophets longed to see.

parts.label: Weeds among the wheat (vv. 24-30, 36-43)
parts.note: An enemy sows weeds, probably a plant that looks like wheat while young, and the owner lets both grow rather than risk pulling up the crop. Jesus explains that good and evil people live side by side in the world until the end, when angels will separate them: the evil are thrown into fire amid weeping and grinding of teeth, and the good shine like the sun.

parts.label: Mustard seed and yeast (vv. 31-35)
parts.note: A tiny mustard seed grows into a plant big enough for birds to perch in, and a little yeast works through a huge batch of dough. These are usually read as pictures of God's rule starting small and hidden but spreading far, and Matthew links this way of teaching to a line from the Psalms.

parts.label: Treasure, pearl and net (vv. 44-52)
parts.note: A man finds buried treasure, a common way to hide valuables then, and a merchant finds a superb pearl, and each gladly sells everything to get it. The net sorting good and bad fish repeats the warning of a final separation, and the closing line is often read as a scripture teacher drawing on both the old Jewish scriptures and Jesus' new teaching.

parts.label: Rejected at home (vv. 53-58)
parts.note: In his hometown, people are amazed by his teaching but cannot get past knowing him as the local carpenter's son with an ordinary family. Jesus says prophets are least honored at home, and their lack of trust means he does few miracles there.

disagreement: Christians differ on why Jesus taught in stories: some stress that the parables hid the truth as a judgment on hardened hearts, while others see them mainly as an invitation that draws in anyone willing to think and ask.
think: Think of an idea or commitment that once grabbed you: what made it either take root in your life or fade away?
